items.title: Deploy the desktop app (Connections, distribution, networking, and auditing) | AWS Quick: Zero to Hero 14
items.summary: Level 200. A handout for IT teams and Quick administrators on deploying the AWS Quick desktop app (AWS Quick on desktop) to company devices. How it works: the three boundaries (the device, the Quick service, and connected apps) and how one request flows through the agent runtime. Turning it on: restrict access with custom permissions first, because adding the desktop connector turns the app on for everyone; sign-in the same way as on the web or with a dedicated IdP; and the Regions with Agentic Features. Deploying it: per-machine installers for macOS (.pkg) and Windows (.exe) with MDM, and the managed policies that turn off social sign-in and automatic updates (DisableSocialLogin, DisableAutoUpdates). Networking and auditing: outbound 443 only, with port 18080 on localhost during sign-in (a diagram); cloud connector calls that start in the Quick service; permissions for local tools such as folder access and browser actions; where data is kept (Quick doesn't encrypt device data, so use FileVault or BitLocker); and AWS CloudTrail, vended logs, and device diagnostics. Three screens of the desktop app show the version, tool permissions, and exporting logs. The rollout order is the author's suggestion, not an official AWS procedure. The appendix has the domains to allow, a glossary, and sources. Based on public documentation as of November 2026. Deck 14 (Roll it out) of the series AWS Quick: Zero to Hero.

items.title: Intro to AWS Quick (An AI assistant for work, on the web, desktop, and mobile) | AWS Quick: Zero to Hero 01
items.summary: Level 100. A handout for anyone starting with AWS Quick, the AI assistant for work on the web, desktop, and mobile. What Quick is: one assistant that answers, creates, acts, and takes on tasks; its four parts (chat, agents, spaces, and integrations); and six features (AWS Quick Sight, Quick Flows, Quick Automate, Quick Research, Apps in Quick, and the desktop app). Where to use it and how to start: the web, desktop, mobile, and extensions; starting at aws.com/quick for people and teams or in the AWS console for companies; and the first screens. Your first request, with a running example of organizing a monthly internal learning session: say what you want, the materials to use, and the format; check the sources cited in the answer; what to do when Quick gets it wrong; and Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and PDF deliverables. What you can ask for: giving Quick materials (attachments, spaces, knowledge bases, local folders), acting in business apps through connectors, and handing work off to Quick Research, Quick Flows, routines, and Quick Automate. The map of Quick, how your data is handled (no plan uses your data to train models; the Tokyo Region as an example), and usage in agent hours. Screens of the web app and the desktop app show the home screens, a request, the sources, and a Word deliverable. The appendix has what each interface supports, the plans, a glossary, and sources. Based on public documentation as of November 2026. Deck 01 (Get started) of the series AWS Quick: Zero to Hero.

items.title: Stop tool calls with rules (Policy in AgentCore and Cedar) | Learn Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Kiro 11
items.summary: This Level 300 deck shows how to stop the tool calls of a help desk agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with rules, using Policy in AgentCore and Cedar. A system prompt covers only the inquiries that go through the agent, so it does not stop a signed-in customer who calls the AgentCore Gateway directly with the same token. Figures with the official AWS icons explain where the policy engine sits on the Gateway, how one MCP tools/call becomes a Cedar request (principal, action, resource and context.input), deny by default and forbid wins, and the schema made from the tool definitions. With real terminal lines from an English copy of the help desk from deck 10 (Amazon Cognito JWT inbound auth), it writes a permit for the 3 shop tools and a forbid on refunds over 30,000 yen unless a store manager asks, makes the same forbid from one English sentence, shows the ALLOW_ALL finding on a rule that allows everyone, and explains why adding both rules in one deploy rolled back. It then attaches the engine in LOG_ONLY (a 54,800 yen refund passed and was counted as a deny in Amazon CloudWatch), switches to ENFORCE (only the customer 54,800 yen refund stopped, both directly and through the help desk), and shows tools/list listing only the tools a caller may call. It also covers temporal policies, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails score conditions, the other places to stop calls (interceptors, rate limits, AWS WAF, Strands Agents Hooks), closing the ways around the rules (IAM rights such as UpdateGateway), and the clean-up. Deck 11 (Govern and share) of the series Learn Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Kiro.

items.title: Less Clicking, More Calling: Building with WebMCP
items.summary: An agent shouldn't need to decipher your page layout to use functionality you've already built.WebMCP lets you expose that functionality as structured tools.In this session, we'll walk through tool registration, progressive disclosure, and the journey to checkout, then compare the results with browser automation.You'll see how little code it can take, where the token savings come from, and where today's agents still need a helping hand.

items.title: Measure whether the harness works (Compare with tasks, trials, and graders) | Learn Harness Engineering with Kiro 10
items.summary: This Level 300 deck, the 10th of Learn Harness Engineering with Kiro, shows how to check whether the harness you added to Kiro (steering, a hook, a skill) works: make tasks from real misses, keep the grading tests out of the workspace, run the same tasks before and after the harness a few times each, and compare scores, transcripts, and cost. On a small booking app built for the series, Kiro CLI headless mode ran 3 tasks 3 times each before and after adding the harness (the 2 feature tasks passed 2 of 6 runs before and 6 of 6 after, at about 2.1 times the credits), and real screens show what that result can and cannot say.

items.title: Connect long work across sessions (Keep the spec, plan, and status in files) | Learn Harness Engineering with Kiro 09
items.summary: When an AI agent works on a long task, no session remembers the last one's conversation and a summary drops details, so this Level 300 deck shows how to keep the spec, plan, runbook, and status in files, read them at the start of each session, do one block of the plan, and hand over a clean state. It uses real screens of Kiro CLI working through the plan of a small booking app over two sessions, with a Session Start hook that runs a smoke test, a Pre Tool Use hook that lets the plan change only its marks, and hooks before and after compaction. This is deck 09 (Run the loop pillar) of the "Learn Harness Engineering with Kiro" series.

items.title: Building Hybrid, Agentic Apps with Apple’s Foundation Models Framework
items.summary: Apple’s Foundation Model framework is the unified API for on-device and cloud-hosted large language models. With it, developers can build intelligent features for their apps that are type-safe, flexible, and leverage existing capabilities of their apps. Learn how to bring intelligent features to your iOS apps using LanguageModelSession and cloud-hosted models like Claude, PCC, and Gemini.
